title: Plate Tectonics
intro: Earth's outer shell is cracked into big slabs called plates. They creep around very slowly, and almost every earthquake, volcano and mountain range is a result of how the plates touch each other. Learn the evidence, the three boundary types (and what each one makes), how to read the seafloor's magnetic stripes, what pushes and pulls the plates, and how hotspots record plate motion.

sections.title: Wegener and continental drift
bullets: **Alfred Wegener** (1880-1930) was a German meteorologist/climatologist. In 1910 he started doubting that **land bridges** (like the Bering Land Bridge) explained why continents share animals and plants.
His idea, **continental drift**: the continents were once joined and then drifted apart.

**Evidence 1, coastline fit**: South America and Africa fit like puzzle pieces (first noticed by Antonio Snider-Pellegrini in **1858**). Wegener got a much better fit by matching the true edge of the continent, the **continental shelf**, not just the coastline.

**Evidence 2, matching fossils**: **Mesosaurus** (aquatic reptile) in both South America and Africa. **Lystrosaurus** (land reptile) in Africa, India and Antarctica. They could not have swum across oceans.
**Evidence 3, glacial deposits** in now-warm places: southern Africa, India, Australia, Arabia.
**Evidence 4, climate/fossil mismatch**: tropical plant fossils in the Arctic Circle.
Opponents said eroded land bridges once linked the continents. But a land bridge tall and long enough to span a whole ocean is physically implausible.

boxes.text: Why do glacial deposits in hot places prove drift? Glaciers need cold climates. If those rocks sit in warm Africa and India today, they were either somewhere colder then, or the continents moved. Land bridges cannot explain a glacier's location, but moving continents can.

Think of a torn photograph. The edges match (coastline), and the picture carries across the tear (fossils, glacial scratches, rock types). A matching picture across a tear means the pieces were once joined.

Wegener was right about the idea (continents move) but wrong about the cause. He had NO credible mechanism. He tried centrifugal force and precession (both later proven wrong). Do not say 'Wegener explained how plates move'.

sections.title: How drift became plate tectonics (1950s to 60s)
bullets: Wegener died in **1930** on a Greenland expedition, still seen as a fringe scientist. The proof came after his death.

**Mapping the ocean floor**: in **1947** researchers adapted **SONAR** to map the mid-Atlantic. **Bruce Heezen and Marie Tharp** made the first detailed ocean-floor map and found the **Mid-Atlantic Ridge**, a basalt mountain range unlike continental mountains.
**1959, Harry Hess**: **seafloor spreading**. Mid-ocean ridges are 'plate factories' that keep making new oceanic crust.
**Transform faults** (perpendicular to ridges) were added later to explain uneven spreading rates. Earthquake epicentres lined up along the ridges.
**Seafloor sediment**: people expected thick, even sediment on an old, fixed seafloor. Instead sediment is **thinner near ridges**, so crust near ridges is **younger** and the seafloor moves.

**Paleomagnetism** = magnetic fields frozen in rock, a 'fossilized compass'. Magnetite in igneous rock lines up with Earth's field while molten, then locks in when it solidifies. It records **inclination** (relates to latitude) and **declination** (relates to magnetic north).
Seafloor surveys showed **symmetric stripes of alternating polarity** on both sides of ridges. By **1963** Hess, **Lawrence Morley** and others used them to support seafloor spreading.
A rock's frozen north often does not match today's magnetic north. Best explanation: **pole movement plus continental movement**.
**Wadati-Benioff zones**: earthquakes trace oceanic plates sinking into the mantle at an angle under trenches and island arcs.
**J. Tuzo Wilson** put it all together: ocean basins open and close (later the **Wilson Cycle**).

boxes.text: Why does thin sediment near a ridge mean young crust? Sediment falls like slow snow. Crust that has been sitting longer collects a thicker blanket. New crust at the ridge has had almost no time, so its blanket is thin. Thin near the ridge, thick far away = crust gets older away from the ridge.
Hess = Hess factory. Ridges are 'plate factories' that print new seafloor, like a conveyor belt that starts at the ridge.

Do not mix up the two Hess-era clues. SEDIMENT thickness says the crust is younger near ridges. MAGNETIC STRIPES say the crust is symmetric and records reversals. Both support spreading. And do not mix up inclination (latitude) with declination (north direction).

sections.title: Layers of the Earth: crust, mantle, core, and lithosphere
bullets: Earth is cut two ways: by **chemical composition** (what it is made of) and by **physical behaviour** (how it acts: rigid or flowing).

**Chemical layers**: **crust** (continental = lower density, granite-like; oceanic = denser, basalt-like), **mantle** (largest by volume, to ~2,900 km, mostly peridotite, an ultramafic rock), **core** (mostly iron and nickel).

The **Moho** (Mohorovicic Discontinuity) is the boundary at the base of the crust. It shows up as a jump in seismic wave speed. Discovered in 1909. Depth: ~5 km under oceans, ~30-40 km under continents.
**Physical layers**: **lithosphere** (rigid outer shell, broken into plates), **asthenosphere** (weak, flows), **mesosphere/lower mantle**, **outer core** (liquid), **inner core** (solid).
The slide figure labels the lithosphere as 'crust and uppermost solid mantle'.
**Oceanic lithosphere**: thin and rigid, ~0 km at ridges up to ~140 km elsewhere. **Continental lithosphere**: thicker (40-280 km) and more plastic at depth.
The **asthenosphere** is mechanically weak and flows by convection driven by core heat. It is relatively continuous (not broken like the lithosphere).

**Outer core** is fully liquid and its circulating iron and nickel is believed to generate Earth's magnetic field. The **inner core** is solid because of immense pressure, despite being the hottest part.

boxes.text: Why can the lithosphere slide on the asthenosphere? The lithosphere is cold and stiff (like a plank). The asthenosphere is hot and weak (like thick toothpaste). A stiff plank rides on soft stuff that can flow, so the plates can move.
Lithos = stone (hard shell). Astheno = 'without strength' (weak). The names tell you the behaviour.

LITHOSPHERE is not the same as CRUST. Lithosphere = crust + the uppermost solid mantle (it is a physical layer). The crust is a chemical layer. Also the asthenosphere is NOT liquid magma: it is solid rock that flows slowly. And a tectonic PLATE is the lithosphere (the plate is 100% lithosphere, not a small share of it). Note: the slide gives the mesosphere depth as ~410-660 km, which is ambiguous because it also calls it the lower mantle; do not memorize that depth.

sections.title: Plates, margins and the three boundary types
bullets: A **plate boundary** is where two plates meet and move relative to each other. This is where quakes, volcanism and mountain building happen.
**Passive margin**: no relative plate motion. Continental lithosphere gradually becomes oceanic lithosphere **within the same plate**. Example: eastern coasts of North and South America.

**Active margin**: oceanic and continental lithosphere belong to **different plates** that move relative to each other. Example: western coasts of North and South America. Most mountain building, quakes and volcanism happen here.
**Three boundary types**: **Convergent** (plates move toward each other), **Divergent** (move apart), **Transform** (slide past each other).
Rule: all volcanoes and quakes sit at boundaries, with ONE big exception: **hotspot** volcanoes (see the Hotspots section).

boxes.text: Why are active margins the busy ones? Two different plates are pushing, pulling or grinding there, so rock gets stressed and cracks (quakes), squeezed up (mountains) or melted (volcanoes). On a passive margin the coast and seafloor ride on the same plate, so nothing grinds.
Passive = Peaceful (same plate). Active = Action (two plates).
'Passive margin' does not mean 'no coast activity today because of weather'. It means no plate boundary. And a coastline is not automatically a plate boundary.

sections.title: Convergent boundaries: subduction
bullets: Convergent = **destructive** boundaries. Two kinds: **subduction** (a denser plate is pushed beneath a more buoyant one) and **collision** (two continents meet).

**Subduction**: dense oceanic lithosphere meets a more buoyant plate (continental, or younger/warmer oceanic) and sinks into the mantle. Global average rate ~**25 miles per million years** (~half an inch per year).
The sinking plate pulls the seafloor into a **trench**, often 2x+ deeper than a typical ocean basin (3-4 km). The **Mariana Trench** is ~11 km deep.

**Accretionary wedge**: seafloor sediment scraped off and piled up between the two plates. Continental fragments on the sinking plate can be stuck onto the wedge as **terranes**. Much of California is built from accreted terranes.

**Magma recipe**: as the slab sinks, heat and pressure squeeze **volatiles** (water, CO2) out of its minerals into the **mantle wedge**. They lower the melting point of the wedge rock, so it melts (**flux melting**). The magma is buoyant, rises and builds a curved **volcanic arc**.

**Two types**: oceanic-continental (Cascades, western Andes) and oceanic-oceanic (Aleutians, Lesser Antilles). In oceanic-oceanic, the older, colder, denser plate sinks under the younger one and may build an **island arc**.
Subduction zones make the **largest earthquakes and tsunamis** (magnitude 9) because their fault surfaces are huge. Examples: 2004 Indian Ocean, 2011 Tohoku.

**Forearc basin**: on the overriding plate between the arc and the trench. **Backarc basin**: behind the arc, formed by tension, sometimes by **slab rollback** (the sinking plate retreats and pulls the overriding plate apart).
**Flat-slab (shallow) subduction** caused the Laramide Orogeny: a low angle means more plate contact, so deformation reaches far from the boundary.

boxes.text: Why does subduction make volcanoes even though the slab is cold? The slab carries water down. Water makes rock melt at a lower temperature, like salt melting ice on a road. The wet mantle wedge melts, the magma is lighter than the rock around it, so it floats up to the surface.
Think of a heavy bowling ball (old oceanic plate) and a wooden board (continent) in water. The dense one always sinks. That is why OCEANIC plates subduct and continents almost never do.

Flux melting (added water) is for SUBDUCTION. Decompression melting (pressure drop) is for RIDGES, RIFTS and hotspots. Another trap: the slide says the slab carries water, but the mantle wedge is the part that melts, not the slab itself.

sections.title: Convergent boundaries: collision and supercontinents
bullets: **Collision**: two continental plates converge (for example when an ocean basin closes). Neither is dense enough to subduct, so they crash instead.

**No subduction = no magma = no volcanism.** Result: tall, **non-volcanic mountains** and broad zones of frequent large earthquakes, sometimes hundreds of km from the boundary (continental lithosphere is more plastic).
When an ocean basin fully closes through subduction, continental collision begins and continents can join into a **supercontinent**.

**Pangaea** formed by collision. Continents seem to gather and split on a cycle of roughly **500 million years**. Pangaea began separating ~200 Ma. It was preceded by **Rodinia** (~1.1 Ga; began breaking up 800-600 Ma).
**Foreland basin**: a dip in the lithosphere pressed down by the weight of a mountain belt (example: Persian Gulf, from the Zagros Mountains).
**Obduction** (rare): a bit of continent is dragged under, but is so buoyant it pops back up, hauling mantle/seafloor slices (**ophiolites**) to the surface.
Collision zones: **Pyrenees**, **Alps**, **Zagros**, **Himalayas** (India into Asia).

boxes.text: Why are the Himalayas not volcanic? Continental rock is too buoyant to sink deep, so no slab pushes water into the mantle, so nothing melts. The crust just gets squeezed upward and piles into mountains.
Two cars of equal weight in a head-on crash: neither goes under the other, so the front crumples up. Crumple = mountains.

A convergent boundary does NOT always have volcanoes. Subduction = volcanoes. Continent-continent collision = mountains but (almost) no volcanoes. Slides say Pangaea began splitting ~200 Ma; the textbook gives Rodinia as 1.1 Ga, same as the slide.

sections.title: Divergent boundaries: rifts and triple junctions
bullets: Divergent = **constructive** boundaries (plates move apart). Two kinds by location: **continental rifts** and **mid-ocean ridges**.
**Rift-to-drift**: a rift widens until it splits the plate, seawater floods in, and the pieces drift apart as separate continents with a new ridge between them.

**Why rifts start**: thick continents reflect heat back into the mantle. Strong convection pushes hot material up against the plate and softens it. Tension stretches and thins the plate and makes **normal (extension) faults**.
Blocks between faults drop to form **grabens** (down-dropped, rift valley) flanked by raised **horsts**. A **half-graben** is when only one side drops.

Rifts avoid old stable interiors (**cratons**). Break-up cracks look like the seams of a soccer ball. Some arms keep spreading, others stall = **failed rift arms**, which can become **aulacogens** (example: Mississippi Valley Embayment).

**Triple junction**: three rift arms stay active near each other, meeting about **120 degrees** apart. Example: **Afar Triangle** (Red Sea ridge, Gulf of Aden ridge, East African Rift). In general a triple junction is a point where **three plate boundaries meet**.
**Narrow rifts**: a few very active boundaries (East African Rift, Lake Baikal). **Broad rifts**: many fault zones over a wide area (Basin and Range).

**Rift volcanism**: smaller, rarer earthquakes and some volcanoes. Magma forms by **decompression melting**: pulling the plate apart lowers pressure, so rock melts. Example: Ol Doinyo Lengai (Tanzania) erupts cool carbonatite lava.

boxes.text: Why does lowering pressure make rock melt? The mantle is already very hot but squeezed by the weight above, which keeps it solid. When the plate stretches and thins, the squeeze lets go and the rock melts, like a shaken soda fizzing when you open it.
Graben = Grave (it goes DOWN). Horst = Hill (it stays UP). Triple junction = the Mercedes logo (three arms, ~120 degrees).

A triple junction is NOT three earthquakes, three passive margins or three normal faults. It is where three plate boundaries intersect. Also, failed rift arms are the ones that STOP spreading, not the ones that continue.

sections.title: Mid-ocean ridges, magnetic stripes and spreading-rate maths
bullets: **Mid-ocean ridges** (**spreading centres**) are the only places that create **new oceanic lithosphere**, by decompression melting of the asthenosphere. Ridge volcanism makes more lava than all other volcanism combined (most is unseen on the deep seafloor).
The ridge is high because new, hot lithosphere is more buoyant (like an ice cube floating). Moving away, it cools, becomes denser and sinks into flat **abyssal plains**.
Two confirmations of spreading: (1) rock age **increases with distance** from the ridge, (2) **thinner sediment** near ridges.

**Magnetic striping (Vine-Matthews-Morley)**: stripes are symmetric on both sides of the ridge. Very hot magma has no magnetic field; as it cools below the **Curie point** it locks in Earth's field direction. Alternating polarity = periodic **reversals** of Earth's magnetic poles.
Stripes are used to reconstruct past tectonics and calculate **spreading rates**.

**Spreading-rate maths**: rate = distance / age, so **age = distance / rate**. Watch units: 1 km = 100,000 cm. Example: a stripe 40 km from the axis, plate moving 2 cm/yr: 4,000,000 cm / 2 cm/yr = **2,000,000 yr = 2 Ma**.

**Hydrothermal vents ('black smokers')**: seawater seeps through hot crust and rises carrying gases and minerals. In 1977 Alvin found life there (tube worms 10+ ft long) living by **chemosynthesis**, not photosynthesis.

boxes.text: Why are the stripes symmetric? New rock forms in the middle, locks in the field direction of the moment, and the ridge splits it in two halves that move away in opposite directions. The same record sits on both sides, like a zipper opening in the middle. Each stripe is a snapshot in time.
Distance divided by speed = time. 40 km at 2 cm/yr: convert 40 km to 4,000,000 cm first. Then split off six zeros: 4,000,000 / 2 = 2,000,000 yr.

Each plate moves 2 cm/yr, so the stripe is 40 km from the axis on ONE side, and age = 40 km / 2 cm/yr = 2 Ma (not 1 Ma and not 4 Ma). Only if the question gave the total opening rate (both sides together) would you divide by the full rate. Also: the ocean floor is YOUNGEST at the ridge, not oldest.

sections.title: Transform boundaries
bullets: Transform = **strike-slip** or **conservative** boundary: plates slide past each other horizontally. **No crust is created or destroyed.**
Direction: stand on one plate and look across. **Dextral (right-lateral)**: the other plate seems to move right. **Sinistral (left-lateral)**: it seems to move left.
Most occur on the ocean floor near mid-ocean ridges as **fracture zones** that handle different spreading rates along the ridge. Some produce no quakes (aseismic).
Some produce major quakes but little mountain building or volcanism: stress builds where plates cannot slide smoothly and is suddenly released.
Most important ones for people are within continents: **San Andreas** (California), **Anatolian** faults (Turkey), **Altyn Tagh** (central Asia), **Alpine Fault** (New Zealand).
**Transpression**: a bend that adds squeezing (**restraining bend**) builds mountains. Example: Big Bend, San Andreas.
**Transtension**: a bend that adds pulling apart (**releasing bend**) makes depressions and sometimes volcanoes. Examples: Dead Sea, Salton Sea.
**Piercing point**: a feature cut and offset by a fault; it helps reconstruct movement. Transform faults keep them intact. The San Andreas has moved over **225 km in the last 20 million years**.

boxes.text: Why almost no volcanoes at transforms? Volcanoes need melting, which needs either pressure drop (ridges, rifts) or added water (subduction). Sliding sideways does neither, so no magma forms. You still get shallow quakes from the grinding.
Dextral = Dexter = right hand. Sinistral = left (think 'sinister' = left in Latin). Transpression = Pressure (squeeze). Transtension = Tension (pull apart).

Transform boundaries do not make new crust or destroy it. Do not call them 'constructive' (that is divergent) or 'destructive' (convergent). On the exam, 'shallow earthquakes but almost no volcanism' = transform fault.

sections.title: What moves the plates, and the Wilson Cycle
bullets: Modern view (slide 2): **convection, gravity and density differences** drive plate motion. The energy is Earth's **internal heat**, not sunlight (textbook: convection currents from interior heat move the plates).

**Wilson Cycle** (J. Tuzo Wilson, 1966): the ongoing birth and breakup of supercontinents (Pangaea, Rodinia). It has run for at least **3 billion years**. Steps: **rifting, ocean basin creation, subduction, basin closure**, then collision builds a new supercontinent.

Why rifting starts: continents reflect heat better than oceans. When continents cluster, more heat goes back into the mantle, convection strengthens and rifts the continent. Some geologists link mantle plumes to those hot periods.
**Three hypotheses** for what drives continents apart and together:
(1) **Ridge push**: after rifting, spreading centres (and convection under them) keep pushing plates apart.
(2) **Slab pull**: sinking slabs at subduction zones pull the rest of the plate along.
(3) **Gravitational sliding**: gravity pulls lithosphere down from the high ridges across the asthenosphere.
Current evidence favours **slab pull** as dominant.
Evidence for slab pull (practice Q3): plates with long subducting edges (Pacific) move much faster than plates with little or no subducting edge (North American).

boxes.text: Why does fast-moving Pacific plate point to slab pull? The Pacific plate has a long sinking edge, and the sinking edge is heavy and drags the plate. The North American plate has hardly any sinking edge and moves slowly. If ridge push were the main force, both would move about the same. Pull strength matches edge length.
Tablecloth: a heavy edge hanging off the table pulls the whole cloth along. The heavy hanging edge is the slab, and the cloth is the plate.

If the Sun stopped shining, plate tectonics would CONTINUE. It runs on Earth's internal heat (convection in the mantle), not solar energy. The planet would freeze, but the plates would still move. Also: ridge push is a hypothesis for the push, slab pull is the 'pull'. Do not swap them.

sections.title: Hotspots and mantle plumes
bullets: A **hotspot** is a fixed area where magma breaks through the lithosphere and makes a volcanic centre. First postulated by **J. Tuzo Wilson in 1963**.
As the plate moves over the stationary hotspot, the old volcano goes **extinct** (no longer over the magma) and a new one forms. Result: a **chain** of islands or mountains.
Hotspots are the **only volcanism not linked to plate boundaries**, with no associated earthquakes. Scientists use eruption ages plus chain shape to calculate plate **speed and direction**.
**Direction rule**: the oldest volcano is farthest from the active hotspot, so the plate has moved **toward the older end** of the chain (if the plume is stationary).
Origin of the magma is debated: deep **mantle plume** near the core, or shallower. Triggers: rifting during supercontinent breakup, subducting slabs, even impacts (a few researchers).
Examples: Tahiti, Afar Triangle, Easter Island, Iceland, Galapagos, Samoa, **Hawaii**, **Yellowstone**.

**Hawaii**: at least 80 million years old; Kilauea erupting continuously since 1983. The **Hawaii-Emperor chain** is ~6,000 km long with a sharp **60 degree bend** ~**50 Ma**, a change in plate motion direction (usually blamed on plate reconfiguration).

**Yellowstone**: under thick continental lithosphere, so eruptions are **less frequent but far more violent**. Track over 15+ million years. Latest big eruption ~**631,000 years ago** (~1,000 km3 of ash and magma).

boxes.text: Why does a hotspot make a chain? Think of a candle flame (plume, fixed) under a sheet of paper (plate) that you slide along. The scorch marks form a line. Each mark is a volcano; the oldest mark is the one furthest along the way the paper moved.
Old volcano = far from the fire. Young volcano = over the fire. The chain 'points' in the direction the plate went.

Hotspots are the exception to 'volcanoes are at plate boundaries'. They are not caused by subduction or rifting. Another trap: the hotspot is stationary and the PLATE moves. Do not say the volcano moved.

cards.front: Who proposed continental drift, and what was the idea?
cards.back: Alfred Wegener (1880-1930), German meteorologist/climatologist. Continents were once joined and drifted apart. He had no working mechanism.

cards.front: Name Wegener's four lines of early evidence.
cards.back: (1) Coastline/continental shelf fit, (2) matching fossils (Mesosaurus, Lystrosaurus), (3) glacial deposits in now-warm regions, (4) tropical plant fossils in the Arctic.

cards.front: Which continental edge gave Wegener a better fit than coastlines?
cards.back: The continental shelf, the true edge of the continent. The coastline-fit idea was first noted by Snider-Pellegrini in 1858.

cards.front: Mesosaurus and Lystrosaurus: where are they found and why does it matter?
cards.back: Mesosaurus (aquatic reptile): South America and Africa. Lystrosaurus (land reptile): Africa, India, Antarctica. They could not swim across oceans, so the continents were joined.
No credible mechanism for how continents moved. He tried centrifugal force and precession, later proven wrong.

cards.front: What actually drives plate motion, per the slides?
cards.back: Convection, gravity and density differences. The energy is Earth's internal heat.

cards.front: Heezen and Tharp, 1947 SONAR: what did they find?
cards.back: The first detailed ocean-floor map, showing the Mid-Atlantic Ridge as a basaltic mountain range unlike continental mountains.
Proposed seafloor spreading: mid-ocean ridges are 'plate factories' continuously making new oceanic crust.

cards.front: What did thinner sediment near ridges show?
cards.back: That crust near ridges is younger than crust farther away, so the seafloor is moving, not fixed.

The study of magnetic fields frozen in rock, a 'fossilized compass'. Magnetite in igneous rock aligns with Earth's field while molten and locks in when solid. Records inclination (latitude) and declination (north).
Angled zones of earthquakes tracing oceanic plates sinking into the mantle under trenches and island arcs.
cards.short: Angled deep quake zones at trenches

cards.front: What did J. Tuzo Wilson contribute?
cards.back: He synthesized the full picture of ocean basins opening and closing (the Wilson Cycle, 1966) and postulated hotspots in 1963.
Crust (continental = granite-like, lower density; oceanic = basalt-like, denser), mantle (largest by volume, to ~2,900 km, peridotite), core (iron and nickel).

cards.front: What is the Moho and how deep is it?
cards.back: Boundary at the base of the crust, a jump in seismic wave speed (found 1909). About 5 km under oceans and 30-40 km under continents.
cards.short: Seismic jump at base of crust

cards.back: The rigid outer physical layer (crust plus uppermost solid mantle), broken into plates. Plate boundaries are where quakes, volcanoes and mountains happen.
cards.short: Rigid outer layer broken into plates

cards.back: The mechanically weak layer under the lithosphere that flows by convection driven by core heat. Relatively continuous.

cards.front: What percentage of a tectonic plate is lithosphere?
cards.back: 100%. A plate is a piece of the broken-up lithosphere.
Oceanic: ~0 km at ridges up to ~140 km elsewhere, thin and rigid. Continental: 40-280 km, thicker and more plastic at depth.
Passive: continent and ocean on the same plate, no relative motion (eastern Americas). Active: they belong to different plates that move (western Americas); most quakes, volcanoes and mountains.
cards.short: Passive: same plate; active: two plates

cards.back: Convergent (toward each other), divergent (apart), transform (slide past).
A denser plate (usually old oceanic lithosphere) is pushed beneath a more buoyant one and sinks into the mantle, at a global average of ~25 miles per million years (about half an inch per year).
cards.short: Dense plate sinks under buoyant one

cards.front: How does subduction make magma (flux melting)?
cards.back: The sinking slab releases water and CO2 into the mantle wedge. Volatiles lower the wedge's melting point, so it melts. The buoyant magma rises and forms a volcanic arc.
cards.short: Water lowers melting point in mantle wedge

cards.back: Trenches can be 2x+ deeper than a typical ocean basin (3-4 km). The Mariana Trench reaches ~11 km.

cards.front: Two types of subduction and examples?
cards.back: Oceanic-continental (Cascades, western Andes) and oceanic-oceanic (Aleutians, Lesser Antilles); in the latter, older denser oceanic plate sinks under younger.

cards.front: Why do subduction zones make the biggest quakes and tsunamis?
cards.back: Only place with fault surfaces large enough for magnitude-9 quakes; a stuck slab suddenly releases energy along hundreds of km. Examples: 2004 Indian Ocean, 2011 Tohoku.
cards.short: Huge fault surfaces make M9 quakes

cards.back: Two continents converge and neither subducts. Result: tall non-volcanic mountains and broad zones of large quakes, no magma (Himalayas, Alps).
Cycle of roughly 500 million years. Pangaea began separating ~200 Ma; Rodinia ~1.1 Ga, broke up 800-600 Ma.
A graben is a down-dropped block between normal faults (rift valley). A horst is the raised block beside it. A half-graben drops on one side only.
Pressure drops when plates pull apart, so hot mantle rock melts. It makes magma at rifts, mid-ocean ridges and (in the practice midterm) hotspots.
cards.short: Pressure drop melts rock at ridges

cards.back: A point where three plate boundaries meet. In rifting: three active rift arms about 120 degrees apart, e.g. the Afar Triangle.
cards.short: Three plate boundaries meet, about 120 degrees

cards.front: Why is a mid-ocean ridge topographically high?
cards.back: New hot lithosphere is buoyant. It then cools, densifies and subsides into abyssal plains with distance.
cards.short: Ridge high because new rock is hot

cards.back: Symmetric stripes of alternating polarity on both sides of ridges. Rock locks in Earth's field as it cools below the Curie point, so stripes record pole reversals and let you calculate spreading rates.

cards.front: How do you find the age of a seafloor stripe?
cards.back: Age = distance from the ridge / spreading rate of one plate. Example: 40 km at 2 cm/yr gives 2 million years.
cards.short: Age equals distance divided by rate

cards.back: Plates slide past horizontally (strike-slip, conservative). No crust created or destroyed. Dextral = other plate appears to move right; sinistral = left. Example: San Andreas.
cards.short: Plates slide past, no crust made or lost

cards.back: Transpression: a bend adds squeezing (restraining bend), builds mountains (Big Bend, San Andreas). Transtension: a bend adds pulling apart (releasing bend), makes basins (Dead Sea, Salton Sea).
A sinking slab at a subduction zone pulls the rest of the plate along. Current evidence favours it as the dominant driving force.
cards.short: Sinking slab drags plate; dominant force

cards.back: Ridge push: spreading centres (and convection) push plates apart after rifting. Gravitational sliding: gravity pulls lithosphere down from the high ridges across the asthenosphere.
cards.short: Ridge push shoves; sliding slides downhill

cards.back: The repeating birth and breakup of supercontinents (Wilson, 1966): rifting, ocean basin creation, subduction, basin closure. At least 3 billion years old.

cards.front: What is a hotspot and how does it show plate motion?
cards.back: A fixed spot where magma breaks through the plate. The plate moves over it, making a chain of volcanoes, oldest farthest from the active one. Ages and shape give plate speed and direction. Not tied to plate boundaries.
cards.short: Fixed magma source leaves volcano chain

cards.back: Hawaii: oceanic lithosphere, gentle and frequent eruptions, Hawaii-Emperor chain ~6,000 km with a 60 degree bend ~50 Ma. Yellowstone: thick continental lithosphere, eruptions less frequent but far more violent, last big one ~631,000 years ago.
cards.short: Yellowstone: rare but violent; Hawaii: frequent

quiz.q: Continents contain rocks over 4 billion years old, but almost no oceanic crust is older than about 200 million years. Why?
options: Old, cold, dense oceanic lithosphere is recycled into the mantle at subduction zones
Ocean currents erode old seafloor away
Old oceanic crust melts at hotspots
Old oceanic crust slowly turns into continental crust
The ocean basins only formed 200 million years ago
quiz.why: New oceanic crust is made at ridges and old, denser oceanic lithosphere sinks back into the mantle at subduction zones, so it is always being recycled. Buoyant continents are not subducted, so they keep very old rocks. (The 200 million year figure is from the practice midterm.)

quiz.q: Which plate boundary typically has shallow earthquakes but almost no volcanism?
options: Mid-ocean ridge
Transform fault
Ocean-continent subduction zone
Ocean-ocean subduction zone
Hotspot
quiz.why: Sliding sideways neither drops pressure nor adds water, so no magma forms, but the grinding makes quakes. Ridges and subduction zones make magma; hotspots have no quakes.

quiz.q: Plates with long subducting edges (like the Pacific plate) move much faster than plates with little or no subducting edge (like the North American plate). This observation best supports which idea?
options: Ridge push is the main force driving plates
Mantle plumes push plates sideways
Slab pull is the main force driving plates
Earth's rotation drags plates westward
Both (a) and (b)
quiz.why: More sinking edge means more pulling, and the plates with more of it go faster. That is slab pull, which the slides say current evidence favours.

quiz.q: A seafloor magnetic stripe sits 40 km from the axis of a mid-ocean ridge. Each plate moves away from the ridge at 2 cm/yr. About how old is the rock in that stripe?
options: 0.5 million years
1 million years
4 million years
2 million years
20 million years
quiz.why: 40 km = 4,000,000 cm. Age = distance / rate = 4,000,000 cm / 2 cm/yr = 2,000,000 years. One plate moves 2 cm/yr, so use that rate.

quiz.q: In a hotspot island chain, the volcanoes get progressively older toward the northwest. If the mantle plume is stationary, which way is the plate moving?
options: Toward the southeast
Toward the northeast
Toward the southwest
The plate is stationary; the plume is moving
Toward the northwest
quiz.why: A volcano forms over the plume and is then carried away by the moving plate. The oldest volcanoes have travelled farthest, so the older end shows where the plate is going: northwest.

quiz.q: The Himalayas sit on a convergent plate boundary, yet they have very few active volcanoes. Why?
options: Continental crust is too buoyant to subduct deeply, so no slab releases water into the mantle
The crust there is too cold to melt
The Himalayas are actually a transform boundary
All the magma escapes through nearby hotspots
The mountains are too tall for magma to reach the top
quiz.why: This is a continent-continent collision. Neither plate sinks, so no water is carried into the mantle wedge, no flux melting, no magma.

quiz.q: A triple junction is ...?
options: a location where three or more earthquakes have occurred.
a point where three plate boundaries intersect.
a point where three passive margins intersect.
a point where three normal faults intersect.
a point where students streaming out of three classrooms collide in the hall.
quiz.why: A triple junction is where three plate boundaries meet, for example the Afar Triangle where three rift arms meet about 120 degrees apart.

quiz.q: What percentage of a tectonic plate is composed of lithosphere?
quiz.why: The lithosphere is broken into segments called plates, so a plate is lithosphere all the way through (crust plus uppermost mantle). It is not a thin layer sitting on a bigger plate.

quiz.q: If the Sun stopped shining would plate tectonics/continental drift continue on the Earth?
options: no
the entire Earth would freeze to a popsicle
only in the southern hemisphere because of a higher proportion of oceanic crust
yes
only in the northern hemisphere
quiz.why: Plate motion is driven by convection in the mantle from Earth's internal heat, plus gravity and density differences, not by sunlight.

quiz.q: Most volcanoes are located at or near plate boundaries, with the big exception being volcanoes that are associated with?
options: oceanic crust
spreading centres
subduction zones
transform faults
hotspots
quiz.why: Hotspots are the only volcanism unrelated to plate boundaries (no link to subduction or rifting).

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT evidence supporting seafloor spreading?
options: Sediment is thickest right at the ridge axis
Rock age increases with distance from the ridge
Magnetic stripes are symmetric on both sides of the ridge
Sediment is thinner near ridges than far from them
Heezen and Tharp found a basaltic mountain range along the Mid-Atlantic
quiz.why: Sediment is THINNER near ridges because the crust is young and has had little time to collect it. The other statements are all evidence.

quiz.q:
Consider these statements about Wegener:
I. He proposed that continents were once joined and then drifted apart.
II. He had a credible mechanism for how continents moved.
III. He improved the coastline fit by using the continental shelf.
options: I only
I and III only
II and III only
all of the above
none of the above
quiz.why: I and III are on the slides. II is false: his biggest flaw was having no credible mechanism (he tried centrifugal force and precession).

quiz.q: Fossils of Lystrosaurus, a land reptile, are found in Africa, India and Antarctica. What does this tell you?
options: Lystrosaurus could swim across oceans easily
Antarctica was always cold and dry
These continents were once joined, since a land animal could not cross oceans
Land bridges as tall as oceans once existed
The fossils were all moved by glaciers
quiz.why: A land reptile could not have swum across oceans, and a land bridge long and tall enough to span an ocean is physically implausible. Joined continents is the simplest explanation.

quiz.q: Which statement about subduction zones is INCORRECT?
options: A denser oceanic plate sinks beneath a more buoyant plate
Water released from the slab lowers the melting point of the mantle wedge
They produce the largest earthquakes and tsunamis on Earth
Magma forms mainly by decompression melting
Trenches can be more than twice as deep as a typical ocean basin
quiz.why: Subduction magma forms by flux melting (volatiles added). Decompression melting is for rifts and ridges.

quiz.q:
Consider these statements about transform boundaries:
I. No crust is created or destroyed.
II. Most occur on the ocean floor around mid-ocean ridges.
III. In dextral motion the opposing plate appears to move to the right.
options: I only
II only
I and II only
II and III only
all of the above
quiz.why: All three are on slide 12: conservative boundaries, mostly at ridges as fracture zones, and dextral = right-lateral.

quiz.q: Why can a supercontinent trigger its own rifting?
options: Continental plates reflect heat back into the mantle better than oceanic plates, so convection strengthens and rifts the continent
Continents are heavier than the mantle and fall into it
Sunlight warms the continent until it cracks
Hotspots always form under supercontinents first
Oceans push against the edge of the supercontinent
quiz.why: Clustered continents reflect more heat into the mantle, giving stronger convection that softens and stretches the plate. This is the proposed rifting mechanism.

quiz.q: Gravitational sliding refers to ...?
options: sinking slabs pulling the rest of the plate along
gravity pulling lithosphere down from the elevated mid-ocean ridges across the asthenosphere
mantle plumes pushing plates sideways
continents sliding along transform faults
sediment sliding into trenches
quiz.why: Option (a) is slab pull. Gravitational sliding is the ridge-to-basin slide across the weak asthenosphere.

quiz.q: In continental rifting, blocks that drop between normal faults are called ...?
options: horsts
aulacogens
grabens
terranes
foreland basins
quiz.why: Down-dropped blocks are grabens; the raised blocks beside them are horsts.

quiz.q: Hotspot volcano A is 500 km from the active hotspot and is 5 million years old. Assuming a stationary plume, about how fast is the plate moving?
options: 1 cm/yr
5 cm/yr
2.5 cm/yr
10 cm/yr
100 cm/yr
quiz.why: 500 km = 50,000,000 cm. Rate = distance / age = 50,000,000 / 5,000,000 = 10 cm/yr. (The numbers are an invented practice example using the slide method.)

quiz.q: Yellowstone eruptions are less frequent but far more violent than Hawaii's. Why?
options: Yellowstone is on a transform boundary
Hawaii has no magma
Yellowstone is at a mid-ocean ridge
Hawaii is much older
The magma has to get through thick, tough continental lithosphere
quiz.why: Continental crust is a much tougher barrier than thin oceanic lithosphere, so pressure builds longer before eruption.

quiz.q: The Hawaii-Emperor seamount chain has a sharp 60 degree bend. What does it mark?
options: A change in plate motion direction about 50 million years ago
The edge of a subduction zone
The start of the Wilson Cycle
A transform fault
A collision with Asia
quiz.why: The bend is usually attributed to a change in plate motion direction ~50 Ma. The slide mentions plume migration as an alternative.

quiz.q: Which statement about margins is correct?
options: Active margins have no relative plate motion
On a passive margin, continental and oceanic lithosphere belong to the same plate
The eastern coasts of the Americas are active margins
Passive margins have the most earthquakes
A passive margin is always a convergent boundary
quiz.why: Passive margins have no relative motion: the continent gradually becomes ocean on the same plate (e.g. eastern coasts of the Americas).

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT associated with continental collision?
options: Tall non-volcanic mountains
Broad zones of large earthquakes
A chain of volcanoes formed by flux melting
A foreland basin
Obduction of ophiolites (rare)
quiz.why: Collision means no subduction, so no flux melting and no volcanic arc. The other features all appear on slide 9.

quiz.q: Why are the magnetic stripes on either side of a mid-ocean ridge symmetric mirror images?
options: Earth's magnetic field is different on each side of the ridge
The stripes are made by hydrothermal vents
Sediment piles up evenly on both sides
New rock forms at the ridge, locks in the field direction as it cools, then splits and moves away in both directions
Plates only move on one side of the ridge
quiz.why: Magma cools below the Curie point at the ridge, locks in the current field direction, then both halves move away. Reversals of Earth's field make the alternating stripes.
